L18@P1: Findings
L19@P1: 1. The Homeless Response Team (HRT) acts in both outreach and
L20@P1: enforcement roles and is impacted by resource constraints in the
L21@P1: City as well as regionally. To help move encampment residents
L22@P1: indoors, the HRT must navigate a complex regional system with
L23@P1: limited shelter and housing resources.
L24@P1: The number of people experiencing homelessness far
L25@P1: exceeded the number of shelter beds in Berkeley in 2024.
L26@P1: Source: Auditor analysis of Alameda County 2024 PIT count and Berkeley
L27@P1: shelter data
L28@P1: 2. The HRT paused some coordination meetings with service
L29@P1: providers due to legal action which resulted in one provider
L30@P1: losing track of clients after encampment actions. The HRT also
L31@P1: had limited access to county information systems shared by other
L32@P1: providers and did not have procedures for collecting encampment
L33@P1: data.
L34@P1: 3. The HRT tracked some outcomes related to their program goals
L35@P1: during the audit period, but did not report on other meaningful
L36@P1: outcomes, such as Coordinated Entry assessments or number of
L37@P1: shelter enrollments. The team’s public reports were also difficult
L38@P1: to access on the City’s website.
L39@P1: Recommendations
L40@P1: To improve coordination and address data inconsistencies, we
L41@P1: recommend the HRT document procedures for coordination with
L42@P1: service providers and data collection, as well as use a shared mapping
L43@P1: tool to assist with coordination. To more effectively measure the
L44@P1: HRT’s impact and enhance transparency, we recommend they
L45@P1: expand on their reported outcomes, consider sharing public reports
L46@P1: in a more accessible format and assess staffing resources needed to
L47@P1: make these improvements.

L100@P2: Introduction
L101@P2: Homelessness is a major crisis in the Bay Area and throughout the United States. The United States Interagency
L102@P2: Council on Homelessness (USICH) acknowledges that no local government alone has the ability or the resources
L103@P2: to completely solve the problem of homelessness. Though the City of Berkeley cannot end homelessness by
L104@P2: itself, meaningfully and sustainably addressing this crisis requires systems to work together, and for
L105@P2: communities to acknowledge their role in contributing to and solving homelessness. In recent years, Berkeley
L106@P2: residents have committed to addressing this issue through tax measures such as Measure P, Measure O, and
L107@P2: Measure W, that allocate resources for purposes including new permanent housing and shelter. Berkeley’s
L108@P2: unsheltered population decreased by 45 percent between February 2022 and January 2024, the largest decrease
L109@P2: among the five largest cities in Alameda County.
L110@P2: We identified the City’s response to homeless encampments as an area for independent analysis due to
L111@P2: community concerns over this issue. We focused on Berkeley’s Homeless Response Team (HRT) because they
L112@P2: are an important touchpoint for people experiencing unsheltered homelessness in Berkeley. While Alameda
L113@P2: County manages and controls access to many homeless resources, the HRT is the interdepartmental city team
L114@P2: that responds to homeless encampments in Berkeley. This audit focuses on the HRT’s operations, data, and
L115@P2-3: reporting; it does not make any recommendations regarding the City’s encampment response policies. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes

L117@P3: Objectives, Scope, and Methodology
L118@P3: Our objectives were to answer the following questions:
L119@P3: 1) What role does the Homeless Response Team have in responding to encampments?
L120@P3: 2) How does the Homeless Response Team coordinate with other organizations to respond to
L121@P3: encampments?
L122@P3: 3) How does the Homeless Response Team use data to measure progress toward goals and how is this
L123@P3: communicated to the public and decision makers?
L124@P3: We evaluated the HRT’s operations between July 1, 2021 – June 30, 2024 (fiscal years 2022 – 2024). We also
L125@P3: reviewed the HRT’s policies, data, outcomes, and public reporting. Additionally, we compared data and
L126@P3: outcomes to best practices from research organizations and other jurisdictions. Lastly, we interviewed city and
L127@P3: county officials, third-party outreach providers and homeless advocates to understand collaboration on
L128@P3: encampment response efforts.
L129@P3: Background
L130@P3: The Berkeley City Council established the HRT in June 2021, and the City Manager’s Office launched the team
L131@P3: in September 2021. The HRT’s initial stated purpose was to respond to homeless encampments in Berkeley by
L132@P3: performing sustained outreach to move people indoors, simultaneously reducing the impact of encampments on
L133@P3: the City with actions such as cleanings or closures that reduce health and safety threats while avoiding citation
L134@P3: and arrest.
L135@P3: Unsheltered homelessness is the result of the nationwide affordable housing crisis that stems from a
L136@P3: combination of increasing rates of deep poverty and a lack of affordable housing.1 Berkeley uses the federally
L137@P3: required point-in-time (PIT) counts to estimate the homeless population, which includes unsheltered and
L138@P3: sheltered individuals.2 Every two years, communities conduct counts of people experiencing homelessness to
L139@P3: measure its prevalence locally. In the January 2024 PIT count in Berkeley, the primary reported causes of
L140@P3: homelessness were related to housing loss (33 percent) and job loss (39 percent) among those surveyed (Figure
L141@P3: 1).
L142@P3: 1 According to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), a person is considered to be experiencing unsheltered
L143@P3: homelessness when they are living in a place not meant for human habitation, including in a tent or impermanent structure within an
L144@P3: encampment.
L145@P3: 2 To measure the sheltered homeless population, Alameda County uses reported occupancy data to count the number of individuals in
L146@P3-4: emergency shelter or transitional housing within Alameda County on the night of the PIT count. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes

L150@P4: Structural racism also contributes to homelessness, as Black/African American and Hispanic & Latino/e/a
L151@P4: individuals are overrepresented among the homeless population nationwide. In Berkeley’s PIT count,
L152@P4: Black/African American residents were 43.8 percent of the homeless population surveyed, compared to only 7.8
L153@P4: percent of Berkeley’s total population (Figure 2).
L154@P4: Encampments refer to individuals or households who are involuntarily unhoused and use temporary shelters,
L155@P4: such as tents, or accumulate large objects on public or City property, according to the HRT’s working
L156@P4: definition.3 People experiencing homelessness may choose to live in encampments for a variety of reasons,
L157@P4: including limited shelter availability or barriers such as shelter rules or conditions that may not meet their
L158@P4: needs. For example, some shelters may have strict entry or exit times, or sobriety requirements. Additionally,
L159@P4: some individuals may have concerns about personal health and safety in shelters, or value the autonomy,
L160@P4: privacy, and sense of community in encampments.4
L161@P4: However, life in encampments also presents significant risks, including hunger, disease, extreme weather, and
L162@P4: violence. Many people living in encampments experience disabling conditions, such as mental or physical health
L163@P4: conditions, or substance use disorders. Among those surveyed as part of Berkeley’s most recent PIT count, 43
L164@P4: percent of people reported having a serious mental illness and 26 percent reported having a substance use
L165@P4: disorder (Figure 2).5
L166@P4: 3 The definition for encampments varies by jurisdiction, as HUD does not have a standard definition for encampments.
L167@P4: 4 A February 2025 investigation by CalMatters found allegations of abuse and dangerous conditions in some California homeless shelters
L168@P4: (‘A volunteer jail’: Inside the scandals and abuse pushing California’s homeless out of shelters).
L169@P4: 5 While some homeless Berkeleyans live in encampments, others may live in other sheltered or unsheltered situations. Berkeley’s total
L170@P4-5: encampment population is unknown. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes

L181@P6: Participants in the study explained that permanent housing would provide the stability they need to find
L182@P6: employment and address physical and behavioral health challenges.6 These findings highlight that access to
L183@P6: affordable housing is crucial in reducing homelessness.
L184@P6: The HRT is a key component of the City’s approach to addressing unsheltered homelessness, though it is only
L185@P6: one piece of a larger regional system. While the HRT’s role is to respond to encampments, encampments will
L186@P6: continue to exist unless sufficient resources are available to prevent people from losing their housing and
L187@P6: permanently house those already experiencing homelessness. Although homelessness prevention is not the
L188@P6: focus of the HRT’s work, it is part of the City’s broader homelessness strategy. By focusing on encampments, the
L189@P6: HRT addresses the visible symptoms of a problem that is much larger than Berkeley itself. The team does not
L190@P6: have the resources to solve homelessness on its own.

L209@P7: Berkeley’s reduction in the number of unsheltered individuals coincides with increased funding to address
L210@P7: homelessness. As a result, Berkeley has been able to open new facilities providing shelter, transitional housing
L211@P7: and permanent housing. The City has also used tax measure funding to apply for and receive state grants to
L212@P7: address homelessness.
L213@P7: The recent reduction in unsheltered homelessness is significant, especially considering that the City does not
L214@P7: exist in a vacuum–regional conditions affect the City’s ability to completely eradicate homelessness. For
L215@P7: example, the needs of unsheltered residents in other Bay Area cities impact Berkeley, as many resources are
L216@P7: shared regionally and predominantly allocated at the county level.
L217@P7: HRT Staff and Funding
L218@P7: The HRT operates within the Neighborhood Services Division of the City Manager’s Office and is overseen by an
L219@P7: Assistant to the City Manager, who also manages the Animal Services, Code Enforcement, and Special Events
L220@P7: units, and oversees homeless policy for the City. The HRT includes a Homeless Response Team Coordinator,
L221@P7: two Social Services Specialists, and a Homeless Services Coordinator (Figure 4).

L224@P7: The HRT also coordinates with other departments to respond to encampments, including Health, Housing and
L225@P7: Community Services; Parks, Recreation and Waterfront; Public Works; Police; Fire; and the City Attorney’s

L286@P10: The legal landscape shapes the City’s encampment actions.
L287@P10: The HRT’s work is also informed by laws, legal precedents, and court orders, along with City ordinances and
L288@P10: policies (Figure 7). The legal landscape that the City operates under includes:

L321@P10: The HRT's internal policy guiding their efforts emphasizes eliminating the worst health and safety impacts with
L322@P10: non-criminal interventions. This policy was developed within the framework of the Ninth Circuit Martin v.
L323@P10: Boise decision (2018), which required jurisdictions to offer shelter to residents before closing encampments.12
L324@P10: 12 This policy also referenced the USICH guidance available at the time, which provides strategies for addressing encampments; updated
L325@P10-11: federal guidance has since been released. Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L326@P11: 12
L327@P11: In June 2024, the Supreme Court altered the legal landscape with its ruling in City of Grants Pass v. Gloria
L328@P11: Johnson et al., which upheld a city’s ability to enforce public camping bans without providing shelter. Following
L329@P11: this decision, the Berkeley City Council adopted an Encampment Policy Resolution in September 2024. This
L330@P11: policy affirmed Berkeley’s continued commitment to offer interim shelter when closing an encampment, but
L331@P11: allowed for exceptions in six specific situations, such as environmental, fire or safety hazards.
L332@P11: All encampment actions must still adhere to federal and state constitutional protections. This includes the
L333@P11: Fourth Amendment, which guards against unreasonable searches and seizures, and the Fourteenth
L334@P11: Amendment, which ensures due process before the government may deprive any person of life, liberty or
L335@P11: property. Encampment actions must also comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act.
L336@P11: Local legal challenges have also affected the City’s encampment operations. The City has been sued multiple
L337@P11: times over their encampment actions. In some of those cases, Temporary Restraining Orders were filed against
L338@P11: the City, which delayed the HRT’s planned encampment actions.
L339@P11: City policies and ordinances also impact how the HRT responds to encampments. For example, Administrative
L340@P11: Regulation 10.1 requires city staff to store property for at least 14 days, with a longer retention period of 45 days
L341@P11: for shelter-related items such as tents and sleeping bags. The regulation also requires city staff to provide at
L342@P11: least 24 hours’ notice before removing unattended property. Administrative Regulation 10.2 provides guidance
L343@P11: around objects placed on sidewalks or parklets. Berkeley Municipal Code ordinances additionally impact the
L344@P11: HRT’s work in encampments (see page 14).
L345@P11: Together, these policies and legal cases influence how the HRT plans and carries out encampment actions.
L346@P11-12:   Homeless Response Team: Opportunities Exist to Strengthen Procedures and Better Track Outcomes
L347@P12: 13
L348@P12: The Homeless Response Team conducts outreach and
L349@P12: enforcement with limited city and county resources.
L350@P12: The HRT works in partnership with other city departments and divisions to respond to encampments, operating
L351@P12: in both an outreach and enforcement role. The HRT works within a complex regional system, with limited
L352@P12: control over shelter and housing referrals managed by the Alameda County CoC. Their efforts are impacted by
L353@P12: resource limitations at both the county and city levels.
L354@P12: The Homeless Response Team acts in both outreach and enforcement roles.
L355@P12: The HRT carries out a range of actions to respond to encampments, operating in both an outreach and
L356@P12: enforcement role (Figure 8). The HRT works with other departments and divisions across the City to address
L357@P12: encampments.

L378@P13: According to the HRT’s internal policy, the HRT evaluates encampments and categorizes their encampment
L379@P13: interventions into low, medium, and high priority levels. The policy does not specify the types of interventions –
L380@P13: such as health and hygiene interventions, public noticing, deep cleanings or closures – used for each priority
L381@P13: level. The highest priority encampments for intervention contain severe hazards such as fire risks or raw
